title: Coriander
wiki_lead:
Coriander (), or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae. The leaves are known as cilantro () in the US. Most people perceive the leaves as having a fresh, slightly citrus taste. Due to variations in the gene OR6A2, some people perceive its flavor to be more soaplike or rotten.
The species is native to the Mediterranean Basin. All parts of the plant are edible, with the fresh leaves and dried seeds most traditionally used in cooking. It is included in Peruvian, Mexican, Indian and Southeast Asian cuisines.
wiki_excerpt:
Coriander (), or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae. The leaves are known as cilantro () in the US. Most people perceive the leaves as having a fresh, slightly citrus taste. Due to variations in the gene OR6A2, some people perceive its flavor to be more soaplike or rotten.
The species is native to the Mediterranean Basin. All parts of the plant are edible, with the fresh leaves and dried seeds most traditionally used in cooking. It is included in Peruvian, Mexican, Indian and Southeast Asian cuisines.


Description

It is a soft plant growing to 50 cm (20 in) tall. The leaves are variable in shape, broadly lobed at the base of the plant, and slender and feathery higher on the flowering stems.
The flowers are borne in small umbels, white or very pale pink, asymmetrical, with the petals pointing away from the centre of the umbel longer (5–6 mm or 3⁄16–1⁄4 in) than those pointing toward it (only 1–3 mm or 1⁄16–1⁄8 in long). The fruit is a globular, dry schizocarp 3–5 mm (1⁄8–3⁄16 in) in diameter. The pollen size is approximately 30 μm (0.0012 in).


Taste and smell

The essential oil from coriander leaves and seeds contains mixed polyphenols and terpenes, including linalool as the major constituent accounting for the aroma and flavour of coriander.
Different people may perceive the taste of coriander leaves differently. Those who enjoy it say it has a refreshing, lemony or lime-like flavour, while those who dislike it have a strong aversion to its pungent taste and smell, characterizing it as soapy or rotten. Studies also show variations in preference among different ethnic groups: 21% of East Asians, 17% of Europeans, and 14% of people of African descent expressed a dislike for coriander, but among the groups where coriander is popular in their cuisine, only 7% of South Asians, 4% of Hispanics, and 3% of Middle Eastern subjects expressed a dislike.
About 80% of identical twins shared the same preference for the herb, but fraternal twins agreed only about half the time, strongly suggesting a genetic component to the preference. In a genetic survey of nearly 30,000 people, two genetic variants linked to the perception of coriander have been found, the more common of which is a gene involved in sensing smells. The gene OR6A2 lies within a cluster of olfactory-receptor genes, and encodes a receptor that is highly sensitive to aldehyde chemicals. Flavour chemists have found that the coriander aroma is created by a half-dozen substances, most of which are aldehydes. Those who dislike the taste are sensitive to the offending unsaturated aldehydes and, at the same time, may be unable to detect the aromatic chemicals that others find pleasant. Association between its taste and several other genes, including a bitter-taste receptor, have also been found.

grok_lead: Coriander ( Coriandrum sativum) is a fast-growing annual herb in the Apiaceae family, native to the Mediterranean region and cultivated worldwide for its edible leaves and seeds. The plant typically reaches a height of 20â70 cm, featuring variable leaves that are broadly lobed at the base and more feathery toward the top, along with small white to pink flowers arranged in umbels. The fresh leaves, commonly known as cilantro or Chinese parsley, provide a distinctive citrusy flavor, while the dried seeds, referred to as coriander spice, offer a warm, nutty taste used in various cuisines. One of the oldest recorded herbs, coriander has been cultivated for over 3,000 years, with evidence from ancient Egyptian tombs and references in texts dating back to 1550 BC. Originating in regions spanning southern Europe, North Africa, and southwestern Asia, it spread globally through trade routes and is now grown in diverse climates, thriving in full sun and well-drained soil with a pH of 6.2â6.8. As an annual, it completes its life cycle in a single growing season, often bolting quickly in warm weather, which influences harvest timing for leaves versus seeds. Coriander's versatility extends to culinary, medicinal, and industrial applications, making it a staple in Latin American, Asian, Indian, and Middle Eastern dishes. The leaves enhance salsas, curries, and soups, while seeds flavor breads, pickles, and sausages; additionally, the plant's essential oils and polyphenols contribute to traditional remedies for digestive issues, inflammation, and antimicrobial effects. Global production, led by India (accounting for nearly 80% of output as of 2023), includes significant contributions from countries like Russia and Morocco, with ongoing research exploring its nutritional profile, including antioxidants and vitamins.
